profile.summary: 2 Samuel narrates David's public ascension to the throne over all the tribes of Israel and shows that his reign was marked by war, covenants, intrigue, and also by the sovereign action of God. Although David was not a perfect king, he sinned seriously with Bathsheba and Uriah - the book insists that the Lord remained committed to him and his offspring. History shows both David's moral and political fragility and the divine fidelity that sustained him, corrected and restored him.
profile.setting: The book takes place in the period of the transition between Saul and David and in the years of David's reign. First, David reigns only in Judah for about seven and a half years, while the north is still divided under the leadership of Isbosete, which generates civil war. Then, with the death of Ishbosheth and the accession of the northern tribes, David transfers his capital from Hebron to Jerusalem, which becomes a political and spiritual center with the arrival of the ark. The reign also involves external conflicts, especially with the Philistines, and internal conflicts later, when David's house faces rebellions and family crisis. The authorship is probably attributed to the same author of 1 Samuel, but this is presented with caution at source; the date is not specified.

structure.label: Fighting for Saul and Early Ascension
structure.description: Death of Saul and Jonathan, I lament David and consolidation of his first dominion in Judah, amid rivalry with Ishbosheth and civil war.

structure.label: Unification and strengthening of the kingdom
structure.description: David takes on Jerusalem as capital, brings the ark, receives the divine covenant, and experiences victories and expansion of the kingdom.

structure.label: Fall with Bathsheba and Divine Discipline
structure.description: David's sin with Bathsheba, the planned death of Uriah, the rebuke of the prophet, and the judgment on the son born of that union.

structure.label: Crisis in the house of David and rebellions
structure.description: Family violence, Absalom's revolt, his attempt to seize the kingdom and then Seba's rebellion against David.

structure.label: Last acts, deliveries and closure of the reign
structure.description: Acts of reparation before the divine wrath, songs upon the power of God and upon the mighty of David, and the census followed by the altar in Jerusalem.

themes: God's faithfulness to his covenant with David and his offspring
The legitimacy of the reign does not depend on the moral perfection of the king, but on God's commitment
Israel's unity advances under the rule of David, despite divisions and rebellions
Sin brings real consequences, including divine discipline and family suffering
The kingdom of David points to a greater king, consummated in Jesus Christ
readingKeys: Notice how the narrative clearly distinguishes between what David does and what God decides, corrects or preserves.
Realize the difference between David's political ascension and the constant fidelity of the Lord to his covenant.
Read the episodes of family conflict and rebellion as a consequence of sin, without losing sight of the book also highlights restoration and continuity of promise.
profile.cautions: The book contains a lot of violence, murders, adultery, sexual abuse and family crisis. The source emphasizes that David is not presented as an impeccable hero: he is guilty of grave sin in a specific case, but not of all deaths linked to his ascension. There is also academic debate about authorship and date, so it is advisable to talk about these issues with prudence.

dossier.narratedEra: The narrative takes place in the transition of the Israel monarchy in David's time: after the death of Saul and Jonathan, during the consolidation of David's reign over Judah and then over all tribes, with civil wars, Philistine threats, territorial expansion and internal crises of the royal house.
dossier.compositionEra: The attached sources do not offer a composition date. They only traditionally claim that the same anonymous author of 1 Samuel probably wrote 2 Samuel, and that the book organizes the history of David's reign with theological and historical focus.

politics.title: From partial ascension to the unification of the kingdom
politics.detail: 2 Samuel portrays David first reigning only over Judah for 7 and a half years, while Ishbosete rules the northern tribes for about 2 years, followed by civil war until the accession of the elders of the north to David.
politics.readingImpact: The reader must see David's coronation not as an immediate and peaceful access to power, but as a slow, conflicting and politically unstable process.

politics.title: Jerusalem as strategic political capital
politics.detail: The capital is moved from Hebron to Jerusalem, described as the best-located center; the conquest of the Jebusites marks the consolidation of David's government.
politics.readingImpact: Jerusalem is not only a later religious scene, but a piece of political and territorial organization of David's monarchy.

politics.title: Decline of the Philistine Threat
politics.detail: The notes highlight that the constant threat of the Philistines, very visible in Judges and Saul, declined widely under the leadership of David, who obtained victories and stabilized the borders.
politics.readingImpact: This helps to read military campaigns as defense and stabilization of the kingdom, not just as aggressive expansion.

politics.title: Dynasties and real legitimacy
politics.detail: The death of Saul, Abner and Ishbosete occurs amid murders and legitimate disputes. The text insists that David did not promote these murders to ascend the throne; on the contrary, he laments Saul and Jonathan and condemns those who killed Saul and Ishbosete.
politics.readingImpact: The reader is directed to distinguish between divine providence in favor of David and the human violence that accompanied the succession crisis.

politics.title: The Davidic Alliance as the axis of government
politics.detail: The book highlights that God made a covenant with David to establish his dynasty, and that the continuity of the throne depends on divine fidelity, not from David's political merit.
politics.readingImpact: The monarchy must be read as an institution submitted to God's promise, not as a simple human dynastic project.

politics.title: Rebellions and seizures of authority
politics.detail: David's reign is crossed by internal revolts: Absalom tries to replace his father, and then Sheba leads another insurrection. The king's own family becomes a center of political instability.
politics.readingImpact: David's power is real, but fragile; the text prepares the reader to understand the fragility of the royal house as part of judgment and providence.

customs.title: Public mourning and honor to the dead
customs.detail: David tears the clothes, weeps and composes for Saul and Jonathan; the practice of public lamentation also appears in the reference to the song preserved in the Book of Jassar.
customs.readingImpact: The suffering of the king and the people must be read according to ancient codes of honor, shame and collective memory.

customs.title: Culture of war and celebration
customs.detail: The note above 1:20 notes that in ancient war culture young women sometimes celebrated victories in songs; announcing the defeat to the Philistines would give them the opportunity to mock Israel.
customs.readingImpact: David's lament poetry works against the logic of war exultation and resists Israel's public humiliation.

customs.title: Meals, wealth and inequality in Nathan's parable
customs.detail: In the parable, the rich possesses flocks, many resources and various wives, while the poor have a single cordeira, a house and no lineage. The scene highlights material and affective asymmetry.
customs.readingImpact: David's guilt becomes more vivid because he, who received much, takes what is the weakest.

customs.title: Wedding, concubinate and real house
customs.detail: The note of 12:8 understands that the "women" given to David can allude to the concubines of Saul's harem; the text also differentiates Bathseba as Urias' wife before being called David's wife.
customs.readingImpact: The reader perceives the real house as a space of inheritance, transfer and dispute, not just of personal romance.

customs.title: Slavery and forced labor after conquest
customs.detail: After the seizure of Rabbah, the defeated Ammonites are made servants and forced to labor; the note associates this with the pattern of submission of peoples overcome in antiquity.
customs.readingImpact: David's military victory includes economic and labor domination, which prevents a romanticized reading of conquest.

customs.title: The eira as a rural and cultured space
customs.detail: The threshing-floor is described as an open space of threshing and jewellery of the cereal; later, this place will become the site of the temple. The note also notes that Araúna was a Jebusite, showing a coexistence of groups in Jerusalem.
customs.readingImpact: The rural context of 24:16-25 illuminates the link between agriculture, worship and the foundation of a sacred national place.

language.title: "Undollar of the Lord" as theological-political title
language.detail: The notes highlight the use of "coroa" and the condition of Saul as "ondo" of God; killing Saul is treated as a serious violation of this consecration.
language.readingImpact: Vocabulary prevents succession from being understood only as a human dispute of power; it has sacral weight.

language.title: The poetic lament as a form of historical interpretation
language.detail: The song of 1:19-27 is read as poetry that exalts honor, defeat, and memory, including with a curse on Gilboa and reference to the "archo" of Jonathan.
language.readingImpact: Poetry guides the reading of the death of Saul and Jonathan as a national tragedy, not a personal triumph of David.

language.title: The Parable as Rare Literary Resource in the Old Testament
language.detail: Nathan's story in 12:1-4 is explicitly described as one of the rare parables of the Old Testament, used to lead David to judgment against himself.
language.readingImpact: The literary form makes the reader experience the process of condemnation before David's confession.

language.title: Word Games and Nomination at 12:3, 24-25
language.detail: The note highlights a parallel between the lamb "as a daughter" and the name Bathseba, in addition to explaining that Solomon probably relates to shalom, and Jedidias means "amateged by Yahweh."
language.readingImpact: These names reinforce themes of affection, peace, and divine election within a house marked by sin and discipline.

language.title: The verb "incitar" and the tension between providence and guilt
language.detail: In 24:1, the note notes that the Hebrew verb used for divine action can mean "inciting" or "instigate," and the case is treated with caution because the source highlights both God's wrath and David's human responsibility.
language.readingImpact: The reader is led to read the census with theological nuance, without simplifying the relationship between divine sovereignty and human sin.

language.title: "Seer" as an ancient term for a prophet
language.detail: The note of 24:11 says that "seer" is an ancient name for a prophet and the differentiating from pagan practices of magic or sorcery.
language.readingImpact: This helps to situate Gade as a legitimate prophetic mediator within the narrative, not as a diviner.

timeline.title: Saul's final fall and the beginning of the royal transition
timeline.detail: The death of Saul and Jonathan at Gilboa ends the forty years of Saul's reign and paves the way for David's public ascension.
timeline.readingImpact: The book begins with a time turn, preparing the reader for dynastic change.

timeline.title: 7 and a half years of reign only in Judah
timeline.detail: The introduction informs that David reigned for 71-2 years over Judah before the accession of the northern tribes; for about 2 years, Ishbosheth reigned in the north.
timeline.readingImpact: The chronology shows that unification was gradual and challenged, not instantaneous.

timeline.title: Conquest of Jerusalem and capital change
timeline.detail: After the death of Ishbosheth, David established Jerusalem as the capital and casts out its Jebusites.
timeline.readingImpact: This milestone alters the reading of Jerusalem as a political and then spiritual center.

timeline.title: Transfer of the ark and sacralization of capital
timeline.detail: The ark is taken to Jerusalem, making the city also the spiritual capital of Israel.
timeline.readingImpact: The ark movement connects government, worship and national identity.

timeline.title: Alliance of Life and Lasting Promitic
timeline.detail: God makes with David an eternal covenant, promising firmness to his house and throne.
timeline.readingImpact: The reader begins to interpret the subsequent history in the light of this promise, including in the crises of the dynasty.

timeline.title: Census, plague and altar in the eira
timeline.detail: The end of the book culminates in the census, in the plague that kills 70,000 people and in the construction of the altar in the eira of Araúna, a place that will later be the site of the temple.
timeline.readingImpact: The outcome links judgment, intercession and the future of national worship in Jerusalem.

investigation: The attached sources are selective and prioritize study notes in key chapters, so several excerpts from the book receive indirect or summarized coverage.
The date of composition is not informed; only traditional authorship is mentioned, without detailed documentary discussion beyond the tradition attributed to the same anonymous author of 1 Samuel.
Some points are interpretations of the commentators, not independent historical evidence; this is especially true for motivational readings, symbolism and theological applications.

There are debated or cautious themes, such as the relationship between divine action and human sin in the census of 2 Sam 24:1, and the possible exact equivalence of certain expressions in 12:8 and 24:31.
The sources do not offer detailed absolute chronology; when there are temporal milestones, they are approximate and linked to the narrative itself.
The dossier does not mix other books without direct support; cross-references appear only when the attached source uses them to explain the text of 2 Samuel.
dossier.limits: This dossier depends solely on the introductions of Tyndale and Matthew Henry and the notes of 2 Samuel 1, 12 and 24. Therefore, historical-cultural coverage is substantial, but not complete: there are missing notes attached to many intermediate chapters, and various statements remain at the level of editorial inference or devotional reading. Tyndale's introduction is more specific about the historical, political, and theology structure of the Davidic dynasty; Matthew Henry is more panoramic and confessional. There is no attempt here to attempt independent historical reconstruction or harmonization beyond what the sources say. Nor should one treat the allusions to wars, customs, names or numbers as external historical proof; they are rather explanations of reading the biblical text itself.
